column2: The Herrimault

The tax carts from the south villages came back empty again. The collectors swear it was the same man each time: a lean outlaw in green with a longbow, who bowed, apologised, took the silver and told them to give the [Root.GetLordLady] his regards. The next morning the silver turned up in the villages, a coin pressed into every widow's hand.\n\nThe peasants call him the Herrimault, the honest outlaw, and they have started to sing about him.
A rogue with manners. Good luck to him.
Every song ends. I will catch him.
A few carts of silver. Let it be.
Someone at court will have something to say about this...
Robbed on the Road

[legend_complainer.GetTitledFirstName] sweeps into the hall with mud on her hem and fury in her eyes. "My [Root.GetLordLady], I was stopped in your own woods by that outlaw and his men! He took my pearls, he took my mother's ring, and then he had the nerve to kiss my hand and call me the fairest robbery of his life. I demand that something be done!" She does not look entirely sorry about the kiss.

[legend_complainer.GetTitledFirstName] stamps into the hall in his shirt and hose. "My [Root.GetLordLady], I was robbed in your own woods! That outlaw took my purse, my horse, my cloak and my boots, and sent me walking home in front of every peasant from here to the river. They laughed! I demand that something be done!"
Here is something for your trouble. Now let me be.
Something will be done. You have my word.
A Trap for the Outlaw

The council has finished with the grain and the roads when my marshal clears his throat. "There is still the matter of the Herrimault, my [Root.GetLordLady]. Half the realm sings about him now. We could ignore him, or we could set a bait he cannot refuse: an archery contest with a silver arrow for the prize. Or..." he glances at my steward, "someone could go into the woods and find him."

I promised the court that something would be done about the Herrimault, and the court has not forgotten. "An archery contest, my [Root.GetLordLady]," my marshal suggests. "A silver arrow for the prize. No bowman alive could stay away. Or someone could go into the woods dressed as a pedlar and find his camp." Everyone looks at me.
Too risky. Leave him be.
Proclaim the contest.
Archers come from every corner of the realm.
Bring me a pedlar's coat. I will go myself.
You set out alone, in disguise.
The Silver Arrow

Banners snap over the lists, and every bowman of the realm is here: yeomen with their longbows, huntsmen in leather, a Tilean crossbowman who has been told twice that this is not that kind of contest. My guards are in the crowd with clubs under their cloaks. Somewhere among these archers is the Herrimault.
Let the shooting begin!
The guards may get their man...
...or the man may get the arrow.
The Outlaw in Chains

He could not resist. The young archer in green split three arrows in a row, and when he stepped up for the silver arrow my guards stepped up with him. Now the Herrimault kneels before me in chains, bruised and smiling, as if this were all part of the joke.\n\n"Hang me if you must, my [Root.GetLordLady]. But every man who has ever sung about me will remember how I died."
Then let them remember. Hang him.
A man who shoots like that is wasted on a rope. Serve me instead.
An Old Man Wins

The silver arrow goes to the last archer anyone expected: a bent old man in a patched cloak who hobbled to the line and put three arrows in the gold so close they split each other. The crowd roared. When I looked again to hand him his prize, he was gone, and so was the arrow.
Wait. Where did he go?
You have a feeling you know.
That Did Not Work

A note was nailed to my door this morning, wrapped around the silver arrow. "My thanks for the prize, [Root.GetLordLady]. It will feed a village through the winter. - H." The court has seen it. The court is laughing behind its hands.
Enough. He has won this round. Leave him be.
Then I go after him myself.
Into the Greenwood

I set out before dawn in a pedlar's coat with a pack of cheap ribbons and knives, a hood over my face and my guards a mile behind. The forest closes in. Every path looks the same, and every crow sounds like a lookout's whistle.
Deeper in.
Your disguise may not hold...
...you may find their camp...
...or you may meet someone on the way.
This was a foolish idea. Home.
Found Out

Lovely ribbons, says the outlaw who steps out of the bushes. "Lovely boots, too. Pedlars do not wear boots like that, my [Root.GetLordLady]." Six more step out behind him with drawn bows. They take my pack, my purse and my boots, turn me around and send me home with a slap on the back. The story is in every tavern before I am.
I will not forget this.
The Outlaws' Camp

Smoke and laughter lead me to a hollow where thirty men and women sit around a fire, roasting a deer that I am fairly sure was mine. A sentry sees me and grins. "A pedlar! Come and sit, friend, there is meat enough for all."
Gladly. I am starving.
You will sit by the outlaws' fire.
I back away slowly...
The Giant on the Bridge

A narrow log bridge crosses the stream, and in the middle of it stands the biggest man I have ever seen, leaning on a quarterstaff as tall as a pike. "Toll is a fall into the water, pedlar," he rumbles. "Yours or mine. Take a staff."
Give me that staff.
You may win...
...you may lose...
...or he may get a look under your hood.
I will find another way across.
Into the River

A feint, a sweep, a lucky crack across the knees, and the giant goes into the stream with a splash that drenches the bank. He comes up spluttering and laughing. "Well struck, pedlar! The Herrimault will want to meet you."
Then lead the way.
Into the River, Again

I last three blows. On the fourth the staff takes my feet out from under me and I go into the water head first. The giant fishes me out by the collar and claps me on the back hard enough to rattle my teeth. "Not bad for a pedlar. Come and dry off by the fire."
My pride is wetter than my clothes.
The Hood Slips

One swing knocks the hood off my head. The giant stares at my face, then at a silver coin he pulls from his belt, then at my face again. "Well, look at that," he says, and then the others come out of the trees. They beat me, they rob me, and they send me home with a split lip and a story nobody at court will ever stop telling.
Ow.
Around the Fire

They sit me down by the fire and give me ale and venison and listen to my lies about the road. The Herrimault himself sits across from me: younger than I expected, quick to laugh, with a bow across his knees. "Tomorrow we ride against the [Root.GetLordLady]'s tax collector," he tells me. "Or there is other work tonight, if you have the stomach for it. You are one of us now, pedlar."
Count me in for the tax collector.
You will rob your own collector.
What is the work tonight?
You will see.
I slip away in the night and bring the guard.
The Herrimault will be brought before you.
I pay for the ale and leave them to it.
The Tax Collector

We take the cart at the ford without a drop of blood spilled. My own collector, a man I appointed myself, kneels in the mud and begs for his life while the Herrimault counts my silver. By nightfall it is gone, handed out coin by coin in villages I did not know were starving.
This has gone too far. Seize them.
I have seen enough. I go home and let them be.
I go home. I know the way to their camp now.
Your soldiers will fall on the camp.
Night Work

At midnight we creep up to the manor of one of my lords, where a poacher hangs in a cage from the gate, left to starve for taking a hare. The outlaws cut him down, carry him off and leave a deer's head on the lord's pillow. The man in the cage was half dead. The lord, I happen to know, is fond of hares.
They have broken my law. Seize them.
This is wrong. I will be back with soldiers.
Ha! That was the best night I have had in years.
You ride home in a very good mood.
I go home and let them be.
The Best Night in Years

I ride home at dawn with twigs in my hair and a grin I cannot get off my face. Nobody at court would believe me if I told them. So I do not tell them. But the next time a lord of mine complains about poachers, I may ask what he did to deserve them.
Long live the Herrimault.
The Outlaw before the Throne

My guards drag the Herrimault in, still in green, still smiling. He looks at my face for a long moment and then laughs out loud. "The pedlar! I should have known by the boots."\n\nThe court waits for my judgement.
You have robbed the crown. You hang.
You have a gift, outlaw. Serve me with it.
Ambush in the Greenwood

My soldiers come at the camp from three sides at dawn. The outlaws fight like cornered wolves, and arrows hiss out of the trees until the last of them is down. In the end the Herrimault stands alone by the cold fire with his bowstring cut and my men all around him.
No quarter. Finish it.
Spare him. Men like these are worth more alive and in my service.
A Wedding in Green

The Herrimault, gamekeeper of my forests now, has asked my leave to marry. The bride is the girl who used to carry messages for the band through my own villages, and who, it turns out, has been in love with him since she was twelve. The whole court comes to the wedding, and a surprising number of my peasants with it.
Long life to the both of you!
The Herrimault and his sweetheart join your court, and will soon wed.
A Rift in the Earth

A shepherd comes to court white as milk and stammering. Out on the hills the ground has split open, a black crack as long as a village, and burning stones fly out of it. The sheep will not go near it. Neither will he.
The ground cracks. It will close again.
Show me.
You ride out to the rift.
Fire and Stones

The rift is wider than the shepherd said. Heat beats up out of it, and every few heartbeats a burning stone the size of a man's head flies out and lands hissing in the grass. The smoke smells of brimstone and of something sweeter that I do not want to put a name to. In the nearest village the people have started to pack.
Keep the people away from it. That is all.
I want to see what is down there.
You go closer to the edge.
The Screaming

Now there are voices. They rise from the rift at dusk, screaming, weeping, begging for help, and the villagers swear they know them: a drowned brother, a mother three winters in the ground. A priest went down on a rope to bless the depths. They pulled the rope back up with nothing on it. The rift must be closed before something climbs out.
Nobody goes near it. Ever.
It must be closed. Whatever it takes.
You must find a way to close the rift.
Closing the Rift

My advisors argue long into the night. The priests want to pray it shut. The steward says the old folk fed such things with cattle until they were full. The master mason wants to fill it with stones. And an old woman from the village, who should not be in my hall at all, says that in her grandmother's day the hungry places were only ever closed by giving them what the realm held most dear.
Let the priests pray it shut.
The priests will pray at the edge of the rift.
Drive the herds into it.
The herds will be driven into the rift.
Fill it with stones.
Every peasant who can push a cart will roll stones into the rift.
Give it what we hold most dear.
The rift will have my heir.
Prayer at the Rift

The priests stand at the edge in a ring, holding their holy symbols out over the smoke, and chant until their voices give out and new priests take their place. On the third day the voices below begin to falter.
Pray on.
The rift may close...
...or it may not.
Stop. There must be another way.
Cattle for the Rift

The herds are driven up from every farm for twenty miles, lowing and stamping, and the drovers whip them on towards the smoke. The rift takes them one after another without a sound. The farmers stand by and count the cost.
Drive them in.
Stop. There must be another way.
Stones for the Rift

Every peasant who can push a cart is set to work. They roll boulders from the hills, tear down old walls and empty the quarry, and tip it all into the smoke. The rift swallows the stones as fast as they come. But it is getting narrower.
Keep rolling!
Stop. There must be another way.
What We Hold Most Dear

[legend_sacrifice.GetFirstName] stands at the edge of the rift beside me. [legend_sacrifice.GetSheHe] does not understand yet why we are here, or why the priests will not meet [legend_sacrifice.GetHerHis] eyes. The voices below have gone quiet. They are waiting.
Forgive me, my child.
No. I cannot do this.
The Rift Is Closed

With a last long sigh, like a sleeper turning over, the earth closes. Where the rift was there is only a scar of black grass, and the hills are silent. The villagers come back to their houses one by one. Nobody will ever graze sheep on that hill again, but nobody will hear the voices either.
The prayers were heard.
It was fed, and it was full.
We buried it.
It had what it wanted.
The Rift Is Still Open
For a day the rift seemed quieter. Then the screaming began again, louder than before, and the fire came back with it. Whatever lives down there was not satisfied.
Then we try something else.
A Burning Rift
A rift full of fire has opened in this ruler's lands.
A Screaming Rift
Voices scream from the burning rift in this ruler's lands.
A Gate to the Abyss
The rift in this ruler's lands is wide open, and something below is waiting.
Prayed the Rift Shut
This ruler's priests closed a burning rift with prayer.
Fed the Rift
This ruler closed a burning rift by feeding it the herds of the realm.
Buried the Rift
This ruler had a burning rift filled with stones by the whole realm.
Gave the Rift Its Due
This ruler closed a burning rift by giving it an heir. People cross the road to avoid them.
Outfoxed by an Outlaw
This ruler was made a fool of by the Herrimault, and the whole realm knows it.
Friend of the Greenwood
This ruler rode with the Herrimault and his band, and the outlaws remember.
Hanged the Herrimault
Let the Herrimault Go
